B03_00: Blood clotting begins when injury or inflammation exposes a procoagulant signal on cells around blood vessels, such as fibroblasts, smooth muscle cells and pericytes, producing an initial burst that primes the clotting cascade. Unrestrained or misplaced activity, including on vesicles shed by tumours or during sepsis, drives thrombosis and disseminated intravascular coagulation, while deficiency of downstream clotting factors causes haemophilia.
B03_01: When a blood vessel is injured, platelets plug the breach and release the contents of their storage granules, amplifying platelet recruitment, supporting clotting and starting wound repair, including new vessel growth and fibrosis. Loss of granule content or of the release machinery causes bleeding disorders such as gray platelet syndrome and storage pool disease, and some immune disorders share the same secretory defects.
B03_02: This ion-signalling step converts receptor stimulation into function in non-excitable cells: in platelets it drives shape change, granule secretion and aggregation during haemostasis, and in lymphocytes it drives immune activation. Inherited loss causes immunodeficiency with impaired platelet and lymphocyte activation, while excessive signalling favours thrombosis, placing this step at the centre of secretion, adhesion and cellular activation.
B03_03: After every signalling transient, cells must restore resting conditions sharply, and this recovery sets the rate of muscle relaxation, especially in the heart, resets neuronal excitability and prepares secretory cells for the next stimulus. It also prevents the sustained overload that triggers cell death. Failure contributes to heart failure, cardiac arrhythmia and hereditary deafness.
B03_04: In activated platelets and other adherent cells, attachment to the surrounding matrix or a clot is converted into growth, survival and migration signals. This link underlies anchorage-dependent growth, cell migration and platelet aggregation during haemostasis; without it, cells remain attached but cannot translate adhesion into proliferative signalling, a property relevant to tissue repair and to how cancer cells escape anchorage requirements.
B03_05: The final protease of the clotting cascade also acts as a hormone-like signal on cells, turning a clotting event into a cellular response. In platelets it drives shape change, granule secretion and aggregation, making it central to haemostasis and arterial thrombosis such as heart attack, and it also affects endothelium, smooth muscle and inflammatory cells. Its receptor is an antiplatelet drug target.
B03_06: Healthy blood vessel lining continuously releases a signal that keeps platelets quiet and vessels relaxed, serving as the main brake on spontaneous thrombosis. The balance between this protective arm and a platelet-derived prothrombotic signal governs bleeding versus clotting tendency. Loss of this tone contributes to pulmonary arterial hypertension and to the thrombotic risk seen with anti-inflammatory drugs that shift the balance.
B03_07: A plasma surface-contact system feeds into blood clotting and links it to inflammation. It is not needed for ordinary haemostasis, since people lacking its initiating factors do not bleed, yet it drives pathological thrombus growth; its deficiency is associated with protection from venous thrombosis, while deficiency of its inhibitor raises thrombotic risk. This makes it an attractive antithrombotic drug target, with platelets providing the assembly surface.
B03_08: A platelet-derived lipid signal drives platelet aggregation and blood vessel constriction, and its overactivity contributes to thrombosis, hypertension and airway constriction. Interrupting its production or blocking its receptor is standard cardiovascular prevention with widely used antiplatelet therapy. Receptor variants found in platelets, placenta and endothelium link this signal to haemostasis and vascular tone.
B03_09: Circulating blood lipid particles at normal plasma levels do not trigger platelets but lower their activation threshold, so that injury signals produce larger aggregation responses. This sensitisation links abnormal blood lipids to the prothrombotic tendency of atherosclerosis and cardiovascular disease. The effect is self-limiting, because the same particles also engage a counteracting restraint that ends the primed state of the platelet.
B03_10: Blood vessels need a signal telling endothelial cells to stay quiescent, attached to each other and alive. The balance of this signal governs vascular stability, permeability and remodelling during development, wound healing and tumour growth. Inherited defects underlie venous malformations, and its dysregulation contributes to blood vessel leak in sepsis and to abnormal tumour vasculature, making it relevant to vascular and cancer therapy.
B03_11: Platelets first stick to a damaged vessel wall through a receptor complex that tethers them under the high shear of arterial blood flow, allowing firm adhesion and activation to follow. Its loss causes Bernard-Soulier syndrome, with giant platelets and bleeding, while inappropriate engagement at ruptured atherosclerotic plaques drives the arterial thrombi behind heart attack and stroke.
B03_12: Platelets release granule contents at sites of vascular injury, and a licensing step governs whether that release can occur, amplifying recruitment and aggregation of further platelets. It sits at the interface of platelet stimulation and regulated secretion. Related control governs hormone release from pancreatic beta cells and granule release from immune cells, and defective granule secretion produces a bleeding tendency.
B03_13: A cell-surface adhesion hub on epithelial and many other cells supports export of metabolic waste from highly glycolytic cells such as tumour cells, and drives neighbouring fibroblasts to produce matrix-degrading enzymes and promote new blood vessels, supporting tumour invasion and metastasis. It also contributes to cell adhesion, energy metabolism, migration and nervous system development, and is studied as a cancer target.
B03_14: Platelets stick to exposed matrix at a damaged vessel wall, and the activation this triggers drives shape change, granule release and aggregation, the first step of haemostasis and a driver of arterial thrombosis. The signalling resembles immune receptor activation in T and B cells. Because loss gives only a mild bleeding tendency, its blockade is pursued as a safer antithrombotic therapy.
B03_15: When platelets and other cells attach to matrix or a clot, this adhesion is converted into growth and motility signals. The outcome is spreading, migration and, in platelets, firm aggregation and clot retraction. Loss of the platelet adhesion receptor or its activation machinery causes bleeding disorders such as Glanzmann thrombasthenia, while invasive tumour cells exploit the same signalling to spread.
B03_16: After injury, an initial trace of clotting activity is amplified into a burst large enough to clot blood, stabilising the platelet plug at the wound with a fibrous mesh. Activated platelets provide the surface for this amplification, and natural inhibitors restrain the burst. Loss of key clotting factors causes haemophilia A and B, while defective inhibition predisposes to venous thrombosis.
B03_17: Activated platelets release a nucleotide that acts back on them to convert a weak, reversible clump into a stable thrombus. This amplification is required for aggregation triggered by every other platelet stimulus and is the target of widely used antiplatelet drugs given after coronary stenting. Inherited loss causes a bleeding tendency, while its activity contributes to arterial thrombosis such as heart attack.
B03_18: A messenger produced in response to vessel-relaxing signals relaxes smooth muscle, restrains platelets and tunes neuronal excitability, and this process covers how its signal acts and is ended. Drugs that prolong the signal sustain vasodilation and are used to treat erectile dysfunction and pulmonary hypertension. Loss of this braking arm favours blood vessel constriction and excessive platelet aggregation.
B03_19: This process liberates precursors of inflammatory lipid mediators and produces the brain's principal endocannabinoid, which suppresses neurotransmitter release at synapses. The balance sets endocannabinoid tone, linking lipid signalling to inflammation, pain and neuroprotection, with platelets as another important site. Inherited loss of one degrading activity causes a neurodegenerative disorder with ataxia, hearing loss, cataract and retinitis pigmentosa.
B03_20: Platelets release a nucleotide that acts back on them to start shape change and the first, reversible wave of aggregation, working alongside a second receptor targeted by widely used antithrombotic drugs. Both arms are needed for full, irreversible aggregation and thrombus stabilisation, so loss of either causes a bleeding tendency, while excess signalling favours arterial thrombosis such as heart attack and stroke.
B03_21: An adhesion receptor concentrated at junctions between endothelial cells, and present on platelets and white blood cells, governs leukocyte migration across vessel walls, T cell activation, platelet responses and new vessel growth. Its signalling is mainly restraining, setting thresholds for platelet aggregation and immune activation, while at junctions it maintains the endothelial barrier and senses blood flow shear, linking it to vascular inflammation and thrombosis.
B03_22: Stress-hormone and sympathetic nerve signalling through this damping receptor arm suppresses pancreatic beta-cell secretion and promotes alpha-cell secretion, contracts gut sphincters, promotes platelet aggregation, and provides presynaptic feedback that limits sympathetic nerve output. That feedback is why drugs acting here lower blood pressure and produce sedation and pain relief, used in hypertension and in anaesthesia and intensive care.
B03_23: Clot formation ends with the conversion of a soluble plasma protein into an insoluble meshwork that seals a wounded vessel and gives the clot mechanical strength, linking platelet aggregation to clot retraction. Built-in brakes keep clotting local. Inherited deficiency of the structural or stabilising components causes bleeding and poor wound healing, whereas loss of the inhibitory arm predisposes to thrombosis.
